definition_en: That system of equipment, network, and personnel to control an unmanned aircraft. Also called UAS.
An aircraft that does not carry a human operator and is capable of flight with or without human remote control. Also called UA.
An unmanned aircraft system whose aircraft weighs less than 55 pounds, together with its ground control station and data links.
notes: Weight threshold as in US civil aviation rules (14 CFR part 107); in doctrine sUAS usually means Groups 1–2.

definition_en: One of five size classes the US military uses for unmanned aircraft, from Group 1 (under 20 pounds, low and slow) to Group 5 (over 1,320 pounds, flying above 18,000 feet).
notes: Groups by maximum weight, operating altitude and speed; table in ATP 3-01.81 ch. 1.

definition_en: A small drone flown by an operator who watches a live video feed from its onboard camera, often through goggles, and often used as a guided explosive weapon.
Loitering munition is a reference to any UAS that can engage beyond line-of-sight ground targets with an explosive warhead or lethal payload to cause injury via a “suicide mode” attack. 1-8.
notes: Defining sentence quoted from the body text.

definition_en: A group of unmanned aircraft that operate together under coordinated or automated control to overwhelm defenses or complete a shared task.
An aircraft that gets lift from wings that do not move, so it must keep moving forward to stay in the air.
An aircraft that gets lift from spinning rotor blades, so it can take off vertically and hover.
A drone lifted by several horizontal propellers (commonly four, six or eight) that lets it hover and change direction quickly.
The equipment, people and procedures used to detect, track, identify and defeat hostile or unauthorized unmanned aircraft.
A defense that places several sensors and weapons at different ranges so that a threat that gets past one layer can still be stopped by the next.
In counter-UAS, the first step: sensing that an aircraft or drone is present, by radar, radio-frequency, optical or acoustic sensors.
notes: The DoD Dictionary entry is the CBRN sense.

definition_en: Precise and continuous position-finding of targets by radar, optical, or other means.

1. The process of determining the friendly or hostile character of an unknown detected contact. 2. In arms control, the process of determining which nation is responsible for the detected violations of any arms control measure. 3. In ground combat operations, discrimination between recognizable objects as being friendly or enemy, or the name that belongs to the object as a member of a class. Also called ID.
In counter-UAS, the step that stops an unmanned aircraft from completing its mission, by destroying it, disabling it or taking control of it.
Stopping an unmanned aircraft by physically hitting it, for example with gunfire, a missile, an interceptor drone or a net.
Stopping an unmanned aircraft without physically hitting it, for example by jamming its control link or its satellite navigation.
Finding a drone by picking up the radio signals passing between it and its controller, which can also point to where the operator is.
A sensor that sends out radio waves and measures their echoes to find the position, speed and direction of objects such as aircraft.
A camera system that uses visible light and heat images to see, follow and identify a target by day or night.
A sensor that detects a drone by listening for the sound of its motors and propellers.
The employment of limited offensive action and counterattacks to deny a contested area or position to the enemy.
Measures taken to reduce the probability of and to minimize the effects of damage caused by hostile action without the intention of taking the initiative.

The deliberate radiation, reradiation, or reflection of electromagnetic energy for the purpose of preventing or reducing the effective use of the electromagnetic spectrum, with the intent of degrading or disrupting combat capability.
Sending false signals, such as fake satellite navigation data, so that a drone or receiver believes it is somewhere it is not.
Actions taken to maintain friendly use of positioning, navigation, and timing information while denying the same to an adversary. Also called NAVWAR.
notes: Covers GNSS/GPS denial. Doctrinal reference: JP 3-14.

definition_en: The production of a beam of concentrated electromagnetic energy or atomic or subatomic particles. Also called DE.
A weapon or system that uses directed energy to incapacitate, damage, or destroy enemy equipment, facilities, and/or personnel.
notes: High-energy laser (HEL); high-power microwave (HPM). Doctrinal reference: JP 3-85.

definition_en: A drone launched to chase and destroy or capture a hostile drone in the air.
Defeating a small drone by catching it in a net fired from the ground or carried by another drone.
The radio connection over which an operator sends commands to an unmanned aircraft and receives its status.
A radio connection that passes data, such as video, position and commands, between an aircraft and the ground or other units.
A range of radio frequencies; many small drones use the 2.4 GHz and 5.8 GHz bands for control and video.
A drone's broadcast of its identity, location and the location of its control station, which receivers on the ground can read.
The place from which a person is controlling a drone; finding it lets security forces stop the threat at its source.
The place from which an unmanned aircraft takes off.
The place where an unmanned aircraft is planned to land or be collected after its flight.
The planned or observed path of an aircraft in altitude, speed and direction over time.
To stay over or near an area for a period of time, for example to watch it or to wait for a target.
The movement of an aircraft into an area toward its target or objective.
The movement of an aircraft out of a target area after completing its task.
An attack by many aircraft, drones or missiles arriving at the same time to overload the defenses.
The point at which more threats arrive than the defense can detect, track or engage at once.
A form of collateral effect that causes unintentional or incidental injury or damage to persons or objects that would not be lawful military targets in the circumstances ruling at the time.
notes: Collateral damage estimate (CDE) is the process that predicts it. Doctrinal reference: JP 3-60.

definition_en: A defined airspace in which a particular weapon system engages air and missile threats. Also called WEZ.
notes: Engagement zone: the general idea; see also missile and fighter engagement zones. Doctrinal reference: JP 3-01.

definition_en: An air and missile defense control measure declared for a particular area and time by an area air defense commander, or delegated subordinate commander, based on the rules of engagement that establish the conditions under which fighters and surface air defense weapons are permitted to engage threats. Also call WCS.
notes: Weapons free / weapons tight / weapons hold. Doctrinal reference: JP 3-01.

definition_en: Weapons free is the least restrictive status: used to indicate when any target not positively identified as friendly in accordance with current ROE may be engaged.
Weapons tight is the normal status. Units may only fire on targets identified as hostile in accordance with current ROE.
Weapons hold is the most restrictive status. Units may only fire in self-defense or when ordered by proper higher authority.

Directives issued by competent military authority that delineate the circumstances and limitations under which United States forces will initiate and/or continue combat engagement with other forces encountered. Also called ROE.

The use of force or other attack against the United States, United States forces, or other designated persons or property to preclude or impede the mission and/or duties of United States forces, including the recovery of United States personnel or vital United States Government property.
The threat of imminent use of force against the United States, United States forces, or other designated persons or property.

An identification derived from observation and analysis of target characteristics, including visual recognition; electronic support systems; non-cooperative target recognition techniques; identification, friend or foe systems; or other physicsbased identification techniques. Also called PID.
The number assigned to an air track so that everyone in the air defense system refers to the same object.

1. A series of related contacts displayed on a data display console or other display device. 2. To display or record the successive positions of a moving object. 3. To lock onto a point of radiation and obtain guidance therefrom. 4. To keep a gun properly aimed or to point a target-locating instrument continuously at a moving target. 5. The actual path of an aircraft above or a ship on the surface of the Earth. 6. One of the two endless belts on which a full-track or half-track vehicle runs. 7. A metal part forming a path for a moving object such as the track around the inside of a vehicle for moving a mounted machine gun.
A single, identical display of relevant information shared by more than one command that facilitates collaborative planning and assists all echelons to achieve situational awareness. Also called COP.
notes: Air picture = the part showing aircraft tracks. Doctrinal reference: JP 3-0.

definition_en: Measures employed to facilitate the efficient use of airspace to accomplish missions and simultaneously provide safeguards for friendly forces. Also called ACMs.
Airspace reserved for specific activities in which the operations of one or more airspace users is restricted. Also called ROZ.
An area where flying drones is prohibited, usually around bases, airports and sensitive sites.
A temporary ban or limit on flights in a defined area, announced to pilots, for example over an emergency or a VIP visit.

An air defense warning given in the form of a color code corresponding to the degree of air raid probability, with yellow standing for when an attack by hostile aircraft or missiles is probable, red for when an attack by hostile aircraft or missiles is imminent or is in progress, and white for when an attack by hostile aircraft or missiles is improbable. Also called ADWC.
notes: Red / yellow / white. Doctrinal reference: JP 3-01.

definition_en: A command and control facility established by the base commander to serve as the focal point for base security and defense. Also called BDOC.

The local military measures, both normal and emergency, required to nullify or reduce the effectiveness of enemy attacks on, or sabotage of, a base to ensure the maximum capacity of its facilities is available to United States forces.
Preventive measures taken to mitigate hostile actions against Department of Defense personnel (including family members), resources, facilities, and critical information. Also called FP.
A Chairman of the Joint Chiefs of Staff-approved standard for identification of and recommended responses to terrorist threats against United States personnel and facilities. Also called FPCON.
A guarded gate where people and vehicles are checked before they are allowed onto an installation.
An area at or near an entry point, set apart from people and buildings, where vehicles are stopped and searched.
The outer boundary of a base or position, usually marked by fences or barriers and watched by guards.
An area of responsibility assigned to a unit; a sector sketch shows its boundaries, positions and fields of fire.
A position from which soldiers watch an area and report what they see.
notes: Listening post: the same at night or by sound.

definition_en: A position placed in front of the defense, usually at night, to give early warning by listening for enemy movement.
A unit kept ready to move at short notice to respond to an incident or reinforce a threatened area.
Duly constituted military, paramilitary, police, and constabulary forces of a state.
A member of a security force on duty protecting a base, its people and its resources.
notes: US Air Force Security Forces call their members Defenders.

definition_en: A detachment sent out to gather information or provide security, on foot (dismounted) or in vehicles (mounted).
A security measure applied at irregular times and places so that an attacker cannot predict the defense.
The distance kept between a possible bomb, such as a vehicle, and the people or buildings it could harm.
Any obstruction or coordinated series of obstacles designed or employed to channel, direct, restrict, delay, or stop movement.
notes: Barrier plan: where barriers go and who closes them. Doctrinal reference: JP 3-15.

definition_en: Measures, such as barriers, film on windows and distance, that reduce the harm an explosion can do.
A posted state that tells everyone on a base whether an attack is unlikely, expected or under way, and what protective action to take.
The check of a base after an attack to find damage, casualties and unexploded ordnance.

Explosive ordnance that has been primed, fused, armed, or otherwise prepared for action and has been fired, dropped, launched, projected, or placed in such a manner as to constitute a hazard to operations, installations, personnel, or material and remains unexploded either by malfunction or design or for any other cause. Also called UXO.
To stay indoors or in the nearest protected place until told it is safe to move.
A reinforced shelter, often of concrete or sandbags, that protects people from blast and fragments.
Cover protects from fire; concealment only hides from view.
Knowing where every person is and whether they are safe, especially after an attack or alarm.
An order that stops all movement on an installation or in a building until the threat has passed.
The announcement that a threat has ended and normal activity may resume.
The person in charge of all response activity at the scene of an incident.
A headquarters for the coordination of information and resources to support incident management activities. Also called EOC.
A system that warns everyone on an installation at once, through sirens, loudspeakers, phones and computers.
Fire, such as mortar, rocket or artillery rounds, aimed at a target the firer cannot see, usually along a high curved path.
C-RAM is a tactical mission that provides detection, warning, C2, and intercept of RAM in flight and engagement of enemy sources of IDF.
notes: Defining sentence quoted from the body text.

definition_en: The risk that a person with authorized access, such as an employee or contractor, uses that access to cause harm.
A nation that allows forces to operate in or to transit through its territory. Also called HN.
Personnel organized and/or employed for security, whether they are civil or military, federal, state or provincial, or local. Also called FSF.
notes: Here: host-nation security forces. Doctrinal reference: JP 3-20.

definition_en: A bilateral or multilateral agreement that defines the legal position of a visiting military force deployed in the territory of a friendly state. Also called SOFA.
The legal authority to investigate, arrest and try people for offenses in a given place.
A citizen of the host country, for example one working on or near a base.
A person assigned to accompany a visitor or contractor who may not move on the base alone.
The list of people authorized to enter a facility or area, checked against their badges.
Passing the current situation, open issues and equipment from one duty shift to the next.
The chronological log in which a security or police desk records incidents and actions.
The written record of everyone who has held a piece of evidence, from collection onward, so it can be trusted.
The exercise of delegated authority over designated airspace and users through control procedures and coordination measures to maximize operational effectiveness.

A method used to task and disseminate to components, subordinate units, and command and control agencies projected sorties, capabilities, or forces for targeting and specific missions. Also called ATO.
Weapons and equipment for actively combating air targets from the ground. Also called ADA.
A device that emits a signal positively identifying it as a friendly. Also called IFF.
notes: Mode 5 = the current secure military IFF mode. Doctrinal reference: JP 3-52.

definition_en: The code an aircraft's transponder sends; 'squawk' is also the order to set that code.
A band of altitudes, between a lower and an upper limit, assigned to one aircraft or activity.
Coordinating times, places and altitudes so that friendly aircraft, drones and fires do not interfere with or endanger each other.
A three-dimensional permissive fire support coordination measure with an associated airspace coordinating measure used to facilitate the integration of fires.

Any combination of characters or pronounceable words, which identifies a communication facility, a command, an authority, an activity, or a unit; used primarily for establishing and maintaining communications. Also called CS.
A code word, which provides no security, that serves the sole purpose of shortening of messages rather than the concealment of their content.
The radio call in which a unit or aircraft reports to a controller that it has arrived and is ready, with its status.
notes: Check-out: the call when it leaves.

definition_en: A report giving the situation in the area of a reporting unit or formation. Also called SITREP.

A concise narrative report of essential information covering events or conditions that may have an immediate and significant effect on current planning and operations that is afforded the most expeditious means of transmission consistent with requisite security. Also called SPOTREP. (Note: In reconnaissance and surveillance usage, spot report is not to be used.)
notes: Often in SALUTE format (size, activity, location, unit, time, equipment). Doctrinal reference: JP 3-09.3.

definition_en: The standard nine-line radio message used to request evacuation of casualties, giving location, frequency, number of patients and other essentials.
A map position given as letters and numbers of a grid system such as MGRS.
The direction to an object measured clockwise from north, in degrees.
notes: Given with range: the distance to it.

definition_en: The actual time at which munitions impact the target. Also called TOT.
A CONTACT whose identity is unknown.

1. [A/A] [AIR-MAR] Positively identified as an enemy in accordance with (IAW) theater ID criteria. The term does not imply direction or authority to engage. 2. * [SO] A SUSPECT whose orbital parameters are such that it may become a collection and/or counterspace concern to a spacecraft in the relative near-term, therefore limiting decision space.

A contact identified as enemy upon which clearance to fire is authorized IAW theater rules of engagement (ROE). WARNING This use of HOSTILE is as a brevity term for air engagements and should not be confused with the same term in tactical data link identification.
A positively identified FRIENDLY aircraft, ship, spacecraft, or ground position.

1. A code meaning “information not available.” 2. An aircraft or ship that has not been determined to be hostile, friendly, or neutral. 3. An identity applied to an evaluated track that has not been identified.
1. [A/A] [A/S] [S/A] Hit observed with valid DWE against a target. 2. * [S/A] [S/S] Informative call to observer or spotter 5 seconds prior to estimated time of impact.
Radar warning receiver indication of an air interceptor threat in track or launch.

1.* [A/A] [A/S] [S/A] [SO] Aircrew does not have visual contact with the TARGET or BANDIT. Opposite of TALLY. 2.* Indicates that radio communications could not be established with the distant end on a specified radio net.
Sighting of a target, non-friendly aircraft, or enemy position. Opposite of NO JOY.
Prebriefed fuel state needed for recovery.
Stop firing, do not open fire. Missiles in flight will continue to intercept; continue to track.

Weapons control status. Fire only: 1. * FREE: at targets not identified as FRIENDLY IAW current ROE. 2. * TIGHT: at targets positively identified as HOSTILE IAW current ROE. 3. * HOLD/SAFE: in self-defense or in response to a formal order. NOTE NATO uses WEAPONS to determine munitions available or remaining, similar to WHAT STATE.
notes: The radio call that sets the weapons control status.

definition_en: Radio procedure word: wait, I will answer shortly.
notes: Procedure word (ACP 125), not a brevity code.

definition_en: Radio procedure word: repeat your last message, or the part named.
Radio transmission received; does not indicate compliance or reaction.
Will comply with received instructions.
Radio procedure words that interrupt traffic on a busy net to pass an urgent message.
The right to give orders and make decisions within a defined area of responsibility.
The action by which a commander assigns part of his or her authority, commensurate with the assigned task, to a subordinate commander.

A commander or individual who has the authority to require consultation between the specific functions or activities involving forces of two or more Services, joint force components, or forces of the same Service or agencies but does not have the authority to compel agreement.
Formal agreement by the person with authority that an action may go ahead.
Contact kept between units or organizations so that they understand each other and act together.
The ability to act together coherently, effectively, and efficiently to achieve tactical, operational, and strategic objectives.
Giving partners the information they need, within the limits of its classification and release rules.
A restriction a nation places on how its forces may be used, or on who may see a piece of information.

The determination that official information requires, in the interests of national security, a specific degree of protection against unauthorized disclosure, coupled with a designation signifying that such a determination has been made.
Formal permission to give classified or controlled information to a partner nation or organization.
A military maneuver or simulated wartime operation involving planning, preparation, and execution that is carried out for the purpose of training and evaluation.
A short, repeated practice of a set procedure so that it becomes automatic.
The imagined situation and events on which an exercise is built.
Lessons learned are validated knowledge and experience derived from observations and the historical study of military training, exercises, and combat operations that lead to a change in behavior.
notes: Defining sentence quoted from the body text.

definition_en: A structured discussion after an event or exercise about what was supposed to happen, what happened, why, and what to do differently.
The commander designated for overall responsibility for airspace control. Also called ACA.
An order implementing the airspace control plan that provides the details of the approved requests for airspace coordinating measures. Also called ACO.
The document approved by the joint force commander that provides specific planning guidance and procedures for the airspace control system for the joint force operational area. Also called ACP.
The planning, coordination, integration, and regulation of airspace by airspace control elements in support of airspace control.
A three-dimensional block of airspace in a target area, established by the appropriate commander, in which friendly aircraft are reasonably safe from friendly surface fires. Also called ACA.
Airspace of defined dimensions within which the ready identification, location, and control of aircraft are required in the interest of security.
A restricted air route of travel specified for use by friendly aircraft and established for the purpose of preventing friendly aircraft from being fired on by friendly forces.
An airspace coordinating measure that uses altitude to separate users and as the transition between different airspace control elements. Also called CA.
Designated areas established by appropriate authority over which flight of aircraft is restricted.
Airspace designated in an airspace control plan or airspace control order in which there is a concentrated employment of numerous and varied weapons and airspace users. Also called HIDACZ.

A method of airspace control that relies on positive identification, tracking, and communicating with aircraft within an airspace, conducted with electronic means by an airspace control element having the authority and responsibility.
A method of airspace control which relies on a combination of previously agreed and promulgated orders and procedures.
The navigable airspace between two points, identified to the extent necessary for the application of flight rules.
The senior command and control element in the Air Force theater air control system’s air, cyberspace, and space operations and coordinates with other components and Services. Also called AOC.
The principal air control agency of the theater air control system responsible for the direction and control of air operations directly supporting the ground combat element. Also called ASOC.
A defined airspace in which surface-to-air missile systems engage air and missile threats. Also called MEZ.
A defined airspace in which surface-to-air missiles and aircraft are simultaneously employed to engage air and missile threats. Also called JEZ.
A defined airspace in which fighters engage air threats. Also called FEZ.
A defined airspace in which low- to mediumaltitude surface-to-air missiles engage air and missile threats. Also called LOMEZ.
A defined airspace in which short-range air defense weapons engage air threats and which may be established within a low- or highaltitude missile engagement zone. Also called SHORADEZ.
A defined airspace in which high-altitude surface-to-air missiles engage air and missile threats. Also called HIMEZ.

1. overseas — A specifically defined airspace for which air defense must be planned and provided. 2. United States — Airspace of defined dimensions designated by the appropriate agency within which the ready control of airborne vehicles is required in the interest of national security during an air defense emergency.
A geographical subdivision of an air defense area.
A geographical subdivision of an air defense region.
A capability that, when added to the basic identification, friend or foe system, provides the means to transmit, receive, and display selected coded replies. Also called SIF.
An identification based on observation and analysis of target behaviors, including location and trajectory, as well as compliance with airspace control measures. Also called procedural ID.
The process of attaining an accurate characterization of detected objects in the operational environment sufficient to support an engagement decision. Also called CID.

An aircraft patrol provided over an objective area, the force protected, the critical area of a combat zone, or in an air defense area, for the purpose of intercepting aircraft before they reach their targets. Also called CAP.
In counterdrug operations, contacts that meet the initial identification criteria applicable in the area where the contacts are detected.
The detection and reporting of enemy activities by an aircraft.
The urgent communication and acknowledgement of time-critical information essential for the preservation of life and/or vital resources.
Direct [active and passive] defensive actions taken to destroy, nullify, or reduce the effectiveness of hostile air and ballistic missile threats against friendly forces and assets. Also called AMD.

The integration of capabilities and overlapping operations to defend the homeland and United States national interests, protect the joint force, and enable freedom of action by negating an enemy’s ability to create adverse effects from their air and missile capabilities. Also called IAMD.
All defensive measures designed to neutralize or destroy enemy forces attempting to penetrate or attack through friendly airspace. Also called DCA.

A mission at the theater level that integrates offensive and defensive operations to attain and maintain a desired degree of control of the air and protection by neutralizing or destroying enemy aircraft and missiles, both before and after launch.
Employment of defense measures to protect limited areas.

The component commander with the preponderance of air defense capability and the required command, control, and communications capabilities who is assigned by the joint force commander to plan and execute integrated air defense operations. Also called AADC.

Commander, subordinate to the area air defense commander, who is responsible for air and missile defenses in the assigned region and exercises authorities as delegated by the area air defense commander. Also called RADC.

Commander, subordinate to an area/regional air defense commander, who is responsible for air and missile defenses in the assigned sector and exercises authorities delegated by the area/regional air defense commander. Also called SADC.
A listing of those assets from the critical asset list prioritized by the joint force commander to be defended with the resources available. Also called DAL.
Defensive measures designed to destroy attacking enemy missiles or to nullify or reduce the effectiveness of such attack. Also called MD.
That degree of control of the air by one force that permits the conduct of its operations at a given time and place without prohibitive interference from air and missile threats.

Air action by aircraft against hostile targets that are in close proximity to friendly forces and that require detailed integration of each air mission with the fire and movement of those forces. Also called CAS.
An officer (aviator/pilot) member of the tactical air control party who, from a forward ground or airborne position, controls aircraft in close air support of ground troops. Also called FAC.
A qualified (certified) Service member who, from a forward position, directs the action of combat aircraft engaged in close air support and other offensive air operations. Also called JTAC.
A subordinate operational component of a tactical air control system designed to provide air liaison to land forces and for the control of aircraft. Also called TACP.
The senior tactical air control party member attached to a ground unit who functions as the primary advisor to the ground commander on air power. Also called ALO.

A joint force commander-validated target or set of targets requiring immediate response because it is a highly lucrative, fleeting target of opportunity or it poses (or will soon pose) a danger to friendly forces. Also called TST.
An entity that performs a function for the adversary or enemy considered for possible engagement.
The process of selecting and prioritizing targets and matching the appropriate response to them, considering operational requirements and capabilities.
Unintentional or incidental effect to an entity that would not be a lawful military target in the circumstances ruling at the time.
The estimate of damage composed of physical and functional damage assessment, as well as target system assessment, resulting from the application of fires. Also called BDA.
An area designated by the appropriate commander into which fires or their effects are prohibited. Also called NFA.

A location in which specific restrictions are imposed and into which fires that exceed those restrictions will not be delivered without coordination with the establishing headquarters. Also called RFA.

A fire support coordination measure established by the land or amphibious force commander to support common objectives within an area of operation, beyond which all fires are coordinated with affected commanders prior to engagement and, short of the line, all fires are coordinated with the establishing commander prior to engagement. Also called FSCL.

A line beyond which conventional surface-to-surface direct fire and indirect fire support means may fire at any time within the boundaries of the establishing headquarters without additional coordination but does not eliminate the responsibility to coordinate the airspace required to conduct the mission. Also called CFL.
The atmosphere, beginning at the Earth’s surface, extending to the altitude where its effects upon operations become negligible.
Defensive measures designed to destroy attacking enemy aircraft or aerodynamic missiles, or to nullify or reduce the effectiveness of such attack. Also called AD.
Defensive measures designed to defeat attacking enemy aircraft and missiles and also negate hostile space systems.

Air operations to perform interdiction conducted at such distances from friendly forces that detailed integration of each air mission with the fire and movement of friendly forces is not required. Also called AI.
A state of aircraft readiness wherein combat-equipped aircraft are airborne and ready for immediate action to reduce reaction time and to increase survivability.
That status in which aircraft on the ground/deck are fully serviced and armed, with combat crews in readiness to take off within a specified period of time after receipt of a mission order.

In antiterrorism, examining the capabilities, intentions, and activities, past and present, of terrorist organizations, as well as the security environment within which friendly forces operate to determine the level of threat.

1. In air and missile defense, a fire control order used to direct or authorize units and/or weapon systems to attack a designated target. See also cease engagement; hold fire. (JP 3-01) 2. To bring the enemy under fire.
1. An attack against an air or missile threat. (JP 3-01) 2. A tactical conflict, usually between opposing lower echelon maneuver forces.
An authority vested with a joint force commander that may be delegated to a subordinate commander, that permits an engagement decision.
The authority and responsibility to engage targets, which may be delegated to subordinate commanders responsible for operational areas. Also called TEA.
An air defense zone established for the protection of key assets or facilities, other than air bases, where weapon systems may be fired at any target not positively recognized as friendly.
The degree of readiness of weapons that can be launched to carry out an assigned task, normally expressed in numbers of weapons and numbers of minutes.
Those minimum actions, including the use of armed force, sufficient to bring a situation under control or to defend against a hostile act or hostile intent.

An operation planned to demonstrate United States resolve that involves increased visibility of United States deployed forces in an attempt to defuse a specific situation that, if allowed to continue, may be detrimental to United States interests or national objectives.

A weapon, device, or munition that is explicitly designed and primarily employed to incapacitate personnel or materiel immediately, while minimizing fatalities, permanent injury to personnel, and undesired damage to property in the target area or environment. Also called NLW.
A fire control order used to direct air defense units to stop tactical action against a specified target.
An emergency fire control order to stop firing on a designated target and destroy missiles in flight.
A specific region into which any weapon system may fire without additional coordination with the establishing headquarters. Also called FFA.
An immediately available, prearranged barrier of fire designed to impede enemy movement across defensive lines or areas. Also called FPF.
Fire delivered on a target using the target itself as a point of aim for either the weapon or the director.
Military action involving the use of electromagnetic energy to control the electromagnetic spectrum or to attack the enemy. Also called EW.

Division of electromagnetic warfare using electromagnetic energy to attack personnel, facilities, or equipment with the intent of deceiving, disrupting, degrading, or destroying enemy combat capability and is considered a form of fires. Also called EA.
Division of electromagnetic warfare that protects personnel, facilities, and equipment from any effects of friendly or enemy use of the electromagnetic spectrum. Also called EP.
Division of electromagnetic warfare involving actions tasked by, or under direct control of, a commander that searches for, intercepts, identifies, and locates electromagnetic energy. Also called ES.

Any electromagnetic disturbance that interrupts, obstructs, or otherwise degrades or limits the effective performance of electromagnetic spectrumdependent systems and electrical equipment. Also called EMI.
Service actions to exploit, attack, protect, and manage the electromagnetic environment. Also called EMSO.
The operational, engineering, and administrative procedures to plan and coordinate operations within the electromagnetic environment.

The ability of systems, equipment, and devices that use the electromagnetic spectrum to operate in their intended environments without causing or suffering unacceptable or unintentional degradation because of electromagnetic radiation or response.
The sum of electromagnetic emissions from all sources that the joint force encounters in a particular operational area. Also called EME.
The intentional insertion of electromagnetic energy into transmission paths in any manner, with the objective of deceiving operators or causing confusion.
Radiation introduced into the devices or systems for the purpose of learning the functions and operational capabilities of the devices or systems.
A strong burst of electromagnetic radiation which may produce damaging current and voltage surges. Also called EMP.

The controlled use of electromagnetic, acoustic, or other emitters to optimize command and control capabilities and minimize detection by enemy sensors, mutual interference among friendly systems, and enemy interference with the ability to execute a military deception plan. Also called EMCON.

This portion of communications security designed to deny unauthorized persons information of value as a result of intercept and analysis of compromising emanations from cryptographic equipment and telecommunications systems.
Protective measures to deny unauthorized access to information of value derived from use of communications systems. Also called COMSEC.
That portion of communications security designed to protect communications from interception and exploitation by means other than cryptanalysis.

A list of TABOO, PROTECTED, and GUARDED functions, nets, and frequencies, sorted by time and location, and limited to the minimum number of frequencies necessary for friendly forces to accomplish objectives. Also called JRFL.

Friendly frequencies used for a particular operation, identified and protected for a period of time to prevent them from being inadvertently jammed by friendly forces while active electromagnetic warfare operations are directed against hostile forces.
The dynamic planning, directing, monitoring, and assessing of operations in the electromagnetic spectrum in support of the commander’s concept of the operation. Also called EMBM.
The characteristics of a system that cause it to suffer a performance degradation when subjected to electromagnetic environmental effects.
Action taken to protect personnel, facilities, and equipment against undesirable effects of electromagnetic energy.
The employment of devices and techniques that impair the effectiveness of enemy actions.
A device or technique employing electrooptical-infrared materials or technology to impair the effectiveness of enemy activity.

That degree of control in the electromagnetic spectrum that permits the conduct of operations at a given time and place without prohibitive interference, while affecting the threat’s ability to do the same.
An air defense zone established around an air base and limited to the engagement envelope of short-range air defense weapons systems defending that base.
A line that delineates the surface area of a base for the purpose of facilitating coordination and deconfliction of operations between adjacent units, formations, or areas.
A collection of bases, geographically grouped for mutual protection and ease of command and control.
A command and control facility that serves as the base cluster commander’s focal point for defense and security of the base cluster. Also called BCOC.

That part of security concerned with physical measures designed to safeguard personnel; to prevent unauthorized access to equipment, installations, material, and documents; and to safeguard them against espionage, sabotage, damage, and theft.

1. Measures taken by a military unit, activity, or installation to protect itself against all acts designed to, or which may, impair its effectiveness. (JP 3-10) 2. A condition that results from the establishment and maintenance of protective measures that ensure a state of inviolability from hostile acts or influences. (JP 3-10) 3. Measures taken to prevent unauthorized persons from having access to information safeguarded in the interest of the nation.
A highly mobile and dedicated security force with the capability to defeat Level I and II threats in a joint security area. Also called MSF.

A rapidly deployable, air-ground, mobile combat unit with appropriate combat support and combat service support assets assigned to, and capable of, defeating Level III threats, including combined arms. Also called TCF.
A specific area to facilitate protection of joint bases and their connecting lines of communications that support joint operations. Also called JSA.
The officer responsible for coordinating the overall security of the operational area in accordance with joint force commander directives and priorities. Also called JSC.
A joint operations center tailored to assist the joint security coordinator in meeting the security requirements in the joint operational area. Also called JSCC.

A Department of Defense intelligence threat assessment of the level of terrorist threat faced by United States personnel and interests in a foreign nation; the levels are expressed as LOW, MODERATE, SIGNIFICANT, and HIGH.
In antiterrorism, a continual process of compiling and examining all available information concerning activities by terrorist groups which could target a facility.
A weapon fabricated or emplaced in an unconventional manner incorporating destructive, lethal, noxious, pyrotechnic, or incendiary chemicals. Also called IED.

A device placed or fabricated in an improvised manner on a vehicle incorporating destructive, lethal, noxious, pyrotechnic, or incendiary chemicals and designed to destroy, incapacitate, harass, or distract. Also called VBIED.
The process to detect, locate, access, diagnose, render safe/neutralize, recover, exploit, and dispose of explosive or improvised explosive threats. Also called EOD.

1. Any material posing a potential threat that contains an explosive component. (JP 3-15) 2. In explosive ordnance disposal, a condition where danger exists because explosives are present that may react in a mishap with potential unacceptable effects to people, property, operational capability, or the environment. Also called EH.
All munitions and improvised or clandestine explosive devices, containing explosives, propellants, nuclear fission or fusion materials, and biological and chemical agents.

The organization, integration, and synchronization of capabilities that enable offensive, defensive, and support activities across the competition continuum to defeat improvised explosive devices. Also called C-IED.
Measures taken before, during, and/or after a hostile action or natural or manmade disasters to reduce the probability of damage and minimize its effects. Also called ADC.
The protection provided to a group of individuals that permits relaxation of individual chemical, biological, radiological, or nuclear protection. Also called COLPRO.

The personal clothing and equipment provided to all military, government civilians, and contractors authorized to accompany the force required to protect an individual from chemical, biological, and radiological hazards and some nuclear hazards. Also called IPE.

A system of protection against chemical, biological, radiological, and nuclear contamination in which personnel are required to wear protective clothing and equipment appropriate to the threat level, work rate imposed by the mission or environment. Also called MOPP.
Department of Defense and non-Department of Defense networked assets and facilities essential to project, support, and sustain military forces and operations worldwide. Also called DCI.

A facility located outside the United States and its territories with little or no permanent United States presence that is maintained by periodic Service, contractor, or host nation support. Also called CSL.
An airfield used to support tactical operations without establishing full support facilities. Also called FOB.
A facility outside the United States and its territories with permanently stationed operating forces and robust infrastructure. Also called MOB.
A tailorable, temporary location used for staging forces, sustainment, and/or extraction into and out of an operational area. Also called ISB.
The state of law and order prevailing within a nation.
All measures, active or passive, taken to counteract hostile surveillance.
An activity that identifies and controls critical information and indicators of friendly force actions. Also called OPSEC.
Cross-functional working group whose purpose is to conduct risk assessment and risk management and to recommend mitigating measures to the commander. Also called FPWG.
Defensive measures used to reduce the vulnerability of individuals and property to terrorist acts, to include rapid containment by local military and civilian forces. Also called AT.

A Department of Defense Service or agency installation within the United States and its territories tasked to serve as a base for military forces engaged in either homeland defense or conducting defense support of civil authorities. Also called BSI.

In base defense operations, a locality from which operations of two or more of the Military Departments are projected or supported and which is manned by significant elements of two or more Military Departments or in which significant elements of two or more Military Departments are located.
A defense strategic intelligence assessment developed by the Defense Intelligence Agency to support combatant command planning. Also called DTA.
The construction of obstacles and emplacement of minefields to delay, disrupt, and destroy the enemy by reinforcement of the terrain.
Devices; systems; and associated tactics, techniques, and procedures designed, fielded, or employed unconventionally.

Preservation of the effectiveness and survivability of mission-related military and nonmilitary personnel, equipment, facilities, information, and infrastructure deployed or located within or outside the boundaries of a given operational area.

Measures to promote, improve, or conserve the behavioral and physical well-being of Service members to enable a healthy and fit force, prevent injury and illness, and protect the force from health hazards. Also called FHP.
The exercise of authority and direction by a properly designated commander over assigned and attached forces in the accomplishment of the mission. Also called C2.

1. The authority that a commander in the armed forces lawfully exercises over subordinates by virtue of rank or assignment. 2. An order given by a commander. 3. A unit or units, an organization, or an area under the authority of one individual.

1. Authority that may be less than full command exercised by a commander over part of the activities of subordinate or other organizations. (JP 1, Volume 2) 2. In mapping, charting, and photogrammetry, a collective term for a system of marks or objects on the Earth, a map, or a photograph, whose positions or elevations (or both) have been or will be determined. (JP 2-0) 3. Physical or psychological pressures exerted with the intent to assure that an agent or group will respond as directed. (JP 3-0) 4. In intelligence usage, an indicator governing the distribution and use of documents, information, or material.

The authority to perform those functions of command over subordinate forces involving organizing and employing commands and forces, assigning tasks, designating objectives, and giving authoritative direction necessary to accomplish the mission. Also called OPCON.

The authority over forces that is limited to the detailed direction and control of movements or maneuvers within the operational area necessary to accomplish missions or tasks assigned. Also called TACON.
Direction or exercise of authority over subordinate or other organizations in respect to administration and support. Also called ADCON.
The succession of commanding officers from a superior to a subordinate through which command is exercised.
A clear and concise expression of the operation’s purpose , key tasks, and military objectives or ends.
Specific information identified by the commander as being essential to facilitate timely decision making. Also called CCIR.
The conduct of military operations through decentralized execution based upon mission-type orders.
The direction of all forces under a single, responsible commander who has the requisite authority to direct and employ those forces.

That authority granted by a commander (any level) to a subordinate to directly consult or coordinate an action with a command or agency within or outside of the granting command. Also called DIRLAUTH.
The planning and synchronization of efforts that occur between elements of Department of Defense and participating United States Government departments and agencies.
A force composed of military elements of nations who have formed an alliance or coalition for a specific purpose. Also called MNF.
A general term applied to a commander who exercises command authority over a military force composed of elements from two or more nations. Also called MNFC.
Official information that has been determined to require, in the interests of national security, protection against unauthorized disclosure and which has been so designated.
In public affairs, the process of reviewing information and products prior to public release to ensure the material does not jeopardize ongoing or future operations.
A communications network that connects an echelon of command with some or all of its subordinate echelons for the purpose of command and control.
The process of fixing, observing, and reporting the location and movement of friendly forces. Also called FFT.
A preliminary notice of an order or action, or a planning directive that initiates the development and evaluation of courses of action by a commander. Also called WARNORD.
A planning directive that provides essential planning guidance and directs the initiation of planning but does not authorize execution. Also called ALERTORD.

1. The commander having primary responsibility for all aspects of a task assigned. 2. In the context of joint planning, the commander who prepares operation plans or operation orders in response to requirements of the Chairman of the Joint Chiefs of Staff. 3. In the context of a support command relationship, the commander who receives assistance from another commander, and who is responsible for ensuring the supporting commander understands the assistance required.

1. A commander who provides actions and other directed support to a supported commander. 2. In the context of a support command relationship, the commander who aids, protects, complements, or sustains another commander’s force and who is responsible for providing the assistance required by the supported commander.
A general term applied to a combatant commander, subordinate unified commander, or joint task force commander. Also called JFC.

A joint force that is constituted and so designated by the Secretary of Defense, a combatant commander, a subordinate unified commander, or an existing joint task force commander to accomplish a specific mission. Also called JTF.
The interrelated responsibilities between commanders, as well as the operational authority exercised by commanders in the chain of command.

In air defense, the normal mode whereby a higher echelon monitors unit actions, making direct target assignments to units only when necessary to ensure proper fire distribution or to prevent engagement of friendly aircraft.
In air defense, the control mode whereby a higher echelon makes direct target assignments to fire units.
Forces trained, equipped, and employed to understand, access, influence, and create effects within the civil component of the operational environment. Also called CA.
Communication activities with external and internal audiences. Also called PA.
Public affairs activities that support the relationship between military and civilian communities.

Contact and interaction between individuals or elements of the Armed Forces of the United States and those of another nation’s armed forces, or foreign and domestic civilian authorities or agencies, to build trust and confidence, share information, coordinate mutual activities, and maintain influence.

Department of Defense interactions with foreign security establishments to build relationships that promote specific United States security interests, develop allied and partner military and security capabilities for self-defense and multinational operations, and provide United States forces with peacetime and contingency access to allies and partners. Also called SC.
The Department of Defense activities that support the development of the capability and capacity of foreign security forces and their supporting institutions. Also called SFA.
Planning and executing the movement and support of forces.
The procurement, distribution, maintenance while in storage, and salvage of supplies, including the determination of kind and quantity of supplies.
Materiel or service support shared with or provided by two or more users. Also called CUL.

Any coordinated logistic activity involving two or more nations supporting a multinational force conducting military operations under the auspices of an alliance or coalition, including those conducted under United Nations mandate. Also called MNL.
Directly assisting, maintaining, supplying, and distributing support of forces at the operating location. Also called BOS.

Civil and/or military assistance rendered by a nation to foreign forces within its territory during peacetime, crises or emergencies, or war based on agreements mutually concluded between nations. Also called HNS.
The creation of temporary facilities for troop support, serving as a base for force projection.
An advanced naval base for the anchoring, fueling, and refitting of transports and cargo ships and for replenishment of mobile service squadrons.
An Army team used to decentralize the execution of movement responsibilities on an area basis or at key transportation nodes. Also called MCT.

term_en: contractors authorized to accompany the force (CAAF)
definition_en: Contractor employees issued a letter of authorization to accompany the joint force in applicable contingency operations outside of the United States. Also called CAAF.
The rapid movement of personnel, materiel, and forces to and from, or within, a theater by air.
Airlift conducted within a theater with forces assigned to a combatant commander or attached to a subordinate joint force commander.
The unloading of personnel or materiel from aircraft in flight.
Any person who is lost to the organization by having been declared dead, duty status – whereabouts unknown, excused absence – whereabouts unknown, missing, ill, or injured.
The unregulated movement of casualties aboard any vehicle. Also called CASEVAC.
The movement of patients under medical supervision to and between medical treatment facilities by air transportation. Also called AE.
Any number of human casualties produced across a period of time that exceeds available medical support capabilities.
The characterization of health support for the distribution of medical resources and capabilities.
A facility established for the purpose of furnishing medical and/or dental care to eligible individuals. Also called MTF.
The deliberate integration of tactics and medicine to treat casualties during combat. Also called TCCC.
Actions to prevent, identify, and manage adverse combat and operational stress reactions. Also called COSC.
The coordination for the movement of patients to match patients with an appropriate medical treatment facility.
Mission-specific protective equipment provided to shield or isolate personnel from hazards. Also called PPE.
Department of Defense activities conducted outside the United States and its territories to directly relieve or reduce human suffering, disease, hunger, or privation. Also called FHA.

Assistance that can be used immediately to alleviate the suffering of foreign disaster victims that normally includes services and commodities, as well as the rescue and evacuation of victims; the provision and transportation of food, water, clothing, medicines, beds, bedding, and temporary shelter; the furnishing of medical equipment and medical and technical personnel; and making repairs to essential services. Also called FDR.

A calamitous situation or event that occurs naturally or through human activities, which threatens or inflicts human suffering on a scale that may warrant emergency relief assistance from the United States Government or from foreign partners.
A situation that poses significant danger to life and property that results from a natural cause.

Assistance to the local populace, specifically authorized by Title 10, United States Code, Section 401, and funded under separate authorities, provided by predominantly United States forces in conjunction with military operations. Also called HCA.
An international and interagency body that coordinates the overall relief strategy and unity of effort among all participants in a large foreign humanitarian assistance operation. Also called HOC.

A temporary center established by a geographic combatant commander to assist with interagency coordination and planning during the early planning and coordination stages of foreign humanitarian assistance operations. Also called HACC.

A team deployed by the United States Agency for International Development, if a large-scale, urgent, and/or extended response is necessary, to provide specialists to assist the chief of mission and the United States Agency for International Development mission (where present) with the management of the United States Government response to a disaster. Also called DART.
The withdrawal of civilians and noncombatants from a threatened area abroad that is carried out with the assistance of the Department of Defense. Also called NEO.

An organization established by a joint force commander to plan and facilitate coordination of activities of the Armed Forces of the United States within local populations and institutions, the private sector, international organizations, nongovernmental organizations, multinational forces, and other governmental agencies. Also called CMOC.
A broad term primarily used by the Department of Defense that includes a displaced person, an evacuee, an internally displaced person, a migrant, a refugee, or a stateless person. Also called DC.
1. Transfer of a patient to or between medical treatment facilities.
Activities that strive to reduce the social, economic, and environmental impact of land mines, unexploded ordnance, and small arms ammunition. Also called HMA.
Fuel state above BINGO at which separation, BUGOUT, or event termination should begin.
No ordnance remaining.
A request to provide information pertinent to the mission in a digital bullseye format unless briefed otherwise.

Inquiry as to the ID of specified track(s), target(s), or correlated GROUP. Responses may include: FRIENDLY, BOGEY, BANDIT, HOSTILE, NEUTRAL, UNABLE, CLEAN, or FURBALL. Full positional data (BULLSEYE) or TRACK NUMBER must accompany responses.
1. [A/A] No sensor information on a GROUP of interest. 2. No visible battle damage. 3. Aircraft not carrying external stores.
No visual contact with FRIENDLY aircraft, ship, or ground position. Opposite of VISUAL.
Sighting of a FRIENDLY aircraft or ground position or ship. Opposite of BLIND.
Cease action or terminate the attack prior to weapons release or event or mission.
Immediate pause of direct or indirect fires. May require coordination to continue.
An emergency fire control order to stop firing on a designated target and destroy missiles in flight. NOTE CEASE FIRE does not destroy missiles in flight.

1. Record the location of a point or object of interest. 2. ** [A/S] [S/S] Spotting round, normally white phosphorus or illumination on the deck to indicate targets to aircraft, ground troops, or fire support. 3. ** [A/A] Challenge and response term for requested aircraft to report contrails.
Radar electromagnetic deceptive jamming.
Electromagnetic communications jamming. NOTE Same as North Atlantic Treaty Organization (NATO) term, CHATTER
Radar indication(s) of noise jamming.
No radar warning receiver indications. unable to engage specified target (e.g., EAGLES NEGATE). Opposite of AFFIRM.
Call to execute launch and leave tactics at a prebriefed range. Modifiers include LONG, SHORT, or QUICK.
Fly at maximum continuous speed.
Fly as quickly as possible, using after-burner or maximum power.
Switch to designated frequency; no acknowledgment required.

1. [A/A] Fighter request for immediate BRAA call (with appropriate fill-ins) to the GROUP described. Indicates fighter intent to intercept or join. 2. [heading] Urgent directive call to turn to a heading. a radar contact inside briefed threat range with BEAM, FLANK, or HOT aspect and is unable to complete sanitization responsibilities implying ownership. A SNAPLOCK call should be responded to with BRAA.
1. [A/S] Acquisition of the reflected laser energy. 2. Platform is laser spot tracker capable.
1. Sensor information at the stated position. 2. [A/S] Acknowledges sighting of a specified reference point (either visually or via sensor). 3. [A/A] Individual radar return within a GROUP or ARM.
Loss of host radar or IR lock-on.
Sensor data is lost on GROUP or CONTACT. Requires information of last known position to include number of CONTACTS and TRACK direction.
1. [A/S] Starting climb for A/S attack. 2. [A/A] Maximum performance climb out of lowaltitude structure.
Sort responsibility within a GROUP has been met.

1. Request for an individual’s tactical situation. 2. * Request for amplifying information on current task or aircraft state (e.g., respond with WORKING, JONESING, CONTACT, CAPTURE, TARGETED, LOCKED, CLEAN, ENGAGED, FUEL (RED/YELLOW/GREEN), WEAPON (RED/YELLOW/GREEN) ready or plain English).

1. ** [A/A] GROUP or CONTACTS direction of flight or movement. 2. ** [A/S] [S/S] Directive call assigning responsibility to an asset for maintaining sensor or visual observation of a defined object or area. 3. ** [A/S] Rotary-wing directive call to establish race track (e.g., “Taz 31, TRACK left). 4. ** [A/S] [AIR-MAR] Information call stating direction of vehicle or CONTACT in motion (e.g., TALLY TECHNICAL TRACK Northwest).
Visual acquisition of a SAM in flight or a SAM launch; should include position.
Untargeted HOSTILE, BANDIT, or BOGEY is within a briefed range of a FRIENDLY aircraft.
Call from an aircraft maneuvering in the visual arena to relinquish deconfliction responsibilities.
1. * [A/A] Intercept the GROUP(S) of interest. 2. * [A/A] Set briefed intercept geometry.
Maneuver to a position on opposite sides, either laterally or vertically from the target.
Perform an immediate maximum performance turn in the indicated direction (default is a 180-degree turn).
In training, shooters are TALLY at assessed missile timeout.

1. FRIENDLY asset is in immediate danger. Withdraw clear in the direction indicated for survival. No further mission support from the FRIENDLY asset is expected. 2. ** [A/A] [S/A] [EW] Cease the intercept and take immediate evasive action. Implies that the target aircraft is being engaged by SAMs or other air defense fighters. 3. ** [A/A] Directive term to instruct air traffic control to clear all civilian or nonengagement aircraft outside a specific area. TERMINATE SCRAM will resume normal operations.
Airborne threat has passed through a defensive layer. Call should include amplifying information.
